1001745.etyen:
Learned borrowing from New Latin trachea (“windpipe, trachea”), continuing Medieval Latin trāchēa (“windpipe, trachea”), from Late Latin trāchīa (“windpipe, trachea”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τρᾱχεῖᾰ (trākheîă, “rough, rugged”), the substantivized feminine of τρᾱχῠ́ς (trākhŭ́s, “rough, rugged”), and an ellipsis of τρᾱχεῖᾰ ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (trākheîă ărtērĭ́ā, “rough artery, windpipe”). The name refers to the cartilaginous rings that give the windpipe an uneven or rough structure.
The Greek adjective is from Proto-Hellenic *tʰrākʰús (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰréh₂gʰ-us (“rough”),

1005073.etyen:
Compound of voll (“rampart”) + bakke (“slope”), literally “rampart slope”.
The first element voll (“rampart”) is from Middle Low German wal (“embankment, rampart”), ultimately from Latin vallum (“rampart, fortification”). The second element bakke (“slope”) is from Old Norse bakki (“bank, ridge, slope”), from Proto-Germanic *bankô (“bank, embankment, hill”).
